chlorpheniramine maleate.note: Can be used during pregnancy when indicated, including the first trimester. May cause sedation.

domperidone maleate.note: Not contraindicated because of pregnancy. Consider when preferred antiemetics fail; assess maternal QT risk.

fexofenadine hydrochloride.note: Reassuring pregnancy data. Loratadine or cetirizine generally preferred because of greater experience.

butamirate citrate.note: First-trimester avoidance is a labeling precaution. In later pregnancy, use only if necessary because human data are limited.

fluconazole.note: Avoid routine oral use in pregnancy. First-trimester and prolonged high-dose exposure are particular concerns. Serious systemic infections may justify specialist use.

hydroxyzine hydrochloride.note: Product labeling advises against use; early-pregnancy restriction and possible neonatal effects near delivery. Human teratogenicity is not established.

ketotifen fumarate (oral).note: Insufficient human pregnancy data to establish safety or harm. Prefer better-studied alternatives; precautionary review.

terbinafine hydrochloride.note: Route-dependent. Topical cream, gel or spray is generally acceptable; oral tablets are not routinely recommended.

ibuprofen.note: Avoid from 20 weeks unless specifically indicated and strongly restrict from 30 weeks.

ivermectin (tablet).note: Avoid routine oral use because safety evidence is limited. Specialist exceptions exist; not proven to be uniformly teratogenic.

aceclofenac.note: NSAID class warning applies from 20 weeks, with stronger restriction from 30 weeks.

rupatadine fumarate.note: Limited pregnancy data do not establish fetal harm. Avoid routinely as a precaution; prefer loratadine or cetirizine.

metformin hydrochloride.note: Can be used for gestational or pre-existing diabetes when appropriate. Insulin is not universally required instead.

diclofenac sodium.note: Systemic NSAID restrictions begin at 20 weeks. Topical formulations require separate assessment.

norethisterone acetate.note: Contraindicated for its usual indications during established pregnancy.

desloratadine.note: Reassuring human pregnancy data, although loratadine or cetirizine is generally preferred.

mecobalamin.note: Vitamin B12 supplementation is acceptable in pregnancy at appropriate therapeutic doses.

tolfenamic acid.note: NSAID precautions apply from 20 weeks, not just the third trimester.

tranexamic acid.note: Not universally contraindicated in pregnancy. May be used for specific obstetric bleeding indications under clinical supervision.

dexibuprofen.note: Same NSAID gestational restrictions as ibuprofen; significant concerns begin at 20 weeks.

losartan potassium.note: Avoid throughout pregnancy; particularly severe fetal renal toxicity during the second and third trimesters.

gliclazide.note: Not recommended for routine diabetes treatment in pregnancy. Insulin-based management generally preferred.

imipramine hydrochloride.note: Not absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Can be continued when clinically justified; monitor for neonatal adaptation effects near delivery.

naproxen sodium.note: Avoid from 20 weeks unless specifically justified, and avoid from approximately 30 weeks.

ketorolac tromethamine.note: NSAID risk begins at 20 weeks; additionally contraindicated during labour and delivery.

cinnarizine.note: Not routinely recommended due to limited human data, but not established as uniformly fetotoxic. Prefer alternatives.

glimepiride.note: Not recommended as routine therapy; switch to more appropriate diabetes management, generally insulin.

tibolone.note: Contraindicated during pregnancy. It is a postmenopausal hormone treatment.

atorvastatin calcium.note: Stop in most pregnancies. Rare high-cardiovascular-risk exceptions require specialist assessment.

aspirin.note: Dose-dependent. Low-dose aspirin is used throughout pregnancy for appropriate indications; analgesic-dose aspirin carries NSAID-type fetal risks.

fenofibrate.note: Not used routinely, but may be considered after the first trimester for severe hypertriglyceridaemia when benefits outweigh risks.

propranolol hydrochloride.note: Can be used during pregnancy when indicated. Monitor fetal growth and possible neonatal bradycardia or hypoglycaemia.

secnidazole.note: First-trimester avoidance appears in some regional labels; limited human evidence does not establish a trimester-specific teratogenic effect.

calcium carbonate.note: Generally safe at recommended doses. Avoid excessive calcium intake.

tiemonium methylsulphate.note: Insufficient human pregnancy safety evidence to classify as established safe. Use only when justified.

calcium orotate.note: Calcium supplementation may be appropriate, but a specific pregnancy hypertension-prevention benefit of calcium orotate is not established.

riboflavin.note: Vitamin B2 is safe at recommended nutritional doses.

allylestrenol.note: Used in some countries for pregnancy-related indications, but not adequate evidence of universal safety or effectiveness. Requires specialist and indication-specific review.

azithromycin dihydrate: Chronic liver disease alone is not a contraindication: Not contraindicated for all chronic liver disease. Contraindicated with previous azithromycin-associated cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction.
diclofenac sodium: Asthma alone is not a contraindication: Asthma alone is not a contraindication. Flag if there is aspirin/NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease.
dexibuprofen: Asthma alone is not a contraindication: Asthma alone is insufficient. Flag if there is previous NSAID-induced bronchospasm or hypersensitivity.
rosuvastatin: Chronic liver disease alone is not a contraindication: Stable compensated liver disease is not itself an absolute contraindication. Flag active hepatic disease or significant unexplained transaminase elevation.
atorvastatin calcium: Chronic liver disease alone is not a contraindication: Stable liver disease alone is not an absolute contraindication. Flag active liver disease or important unexplained hepatic injury.

interaction_not_major.note: No established major interaction between these oral drugs.
Not a major interaction. A moderate absorption interaction may occur; separate administration by about 2 hours and monitor glucose.
Not a major interaction. Calcium carbonate can reduce atenolol absorption; separate administration by at least 2 hours and monitor response.
